solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Gunner has job to patrol foreign city

indicators.note: to patrol is to move around an area, so the letters of the three words before are moved around into a new order

explanation.surface: An artilleryman has been given the job of patrolling a city overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to patrol' looks like the soldier's duty, but 'patrol' is the anagram signal working on GUNNER HAS JOB.
explanation.definitionFit: Johannesburg is South Africa's largest city, so to a British setter it is an example of a city abroad.

clue.text: Extra provision of meals in the Mediterranean, perhaps

parts.note: over can mean extra or surplus, as in left over
board is meals provided, as in bed and board

explanation.surface: A hotel offering extra meals somewhere around the Mediterranean.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads like a holiday location; in fact it describes something that has fallen from a ship into the sea, with 'perhaps' marking the Mediterranean as just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that has gone over the side of a ship is in the sea, and the Mediterranean is one such sea.

clue.text: A speaker and others certain to be great

parts.note: we is the pronoun a speaker uses for themselves together with others
some means certain, as in certain people or some people

explanation.surface: A speaker and the rest are sure to be magnificent.
explanation.definitionFit: In modern informal use both words are terms of high praise meaning excellent or wonderful.

clue.text: To jog — not good without clothing

indicators.note: not here tells us to leave out the letter for good from the word before

parts.note: to jog someone is to nudge them, as in jogging their elbow

explanation.surface: Going for a run, which isn't good when done naked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To jog' suggests running, but here it means to give a little push.
explanation.definitionFit: Being naked means wearing no clothes at all, a straight synonym.

clue.text: Athlete to break away, having transferred left to right

indicators.note: transferred from one thing to another signals swapping one letter for another in the word

parts.note: a group that breaks away from a party is said to splinter

explanation.surface: A runner breaking clear of the pack after moving from the left side to the right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having transferred left to right' tells us to replace the L in SPLINTER with an R.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprinter is a short-distance runner, a specific kind of athlete.

clue.text: At college, drunk and anxious

parts.note: in British usage a student who is up is in residence at university
tight is informal for drunk

explanation.surface: A student at university, drunk and nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: Being 'up' at Oxford or Cambridge is the British idiom for being in residence at university.
explanation.definitionFit: Tense and nervous is the informal sense of the word, a direct synonym for worried.

clue.text: Clearing boy arrested by extremists in gendarmerie

indicators.note: arrested by suggests being held inside, so the boy goes between the other letters
the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A boy is cleared after being arrested by extremists in the French police.
explanation.walkthrough: The gendarmerie is the French police force; only its outer letters G and E are used.
explanation.definitionFit: An open space in a wood free of trees is a glade, so the noun sense of clearing fits.

clue.text: Plant container — upended cask with support broken by rook

parts.note: a chest is a box for storing things

indicators.note: upended in a down clue means the word is turned upside down, read bottom to top

parts.note: a tun is a large cask for wine or beer

indicators.note: broken by means the next letter is inserted into the word, splitting it

parts.note: a tee is the peg supporting a golf ball
R is the chess abbreviation for rook

explanation.surface: Describing a container: a barrel turned upside down, propped up and smashed by a chess piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upended' turns TUN into NUT; 'broken by' puts R into TEE to make TREE.
explanation.definitionFit: A chestnut is a large tree, and any tree is a kind of plant.

clue.text: Fraud before bid

parts.note: pre is a prefix meaning before
a tender is a formal bid or offer for a contract

explanation.surface: A con trick made ahead of an offer.
explanation.definitionFit: A pretender falsely claims a title or quality, making them an impostor or fake.

clue.text: Sign of gratitude from giving postman a lift

parts.note: Postman Pat is the title character of a British children's TV series
giving someone a lift on the back is a piggyback; carrying a person on the back lifts them

explanation.surface: Thanks received for giving a mail carrier a ride.
explanation.walkthrough: Postman Pat is a long-running British children's programme about a village postman; carrying him on your back gives the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A pat on the back is an idiom for praise or congratulation, a gesture showing appreciation.

clue.text: Get rid of skin complaint after time

indicators.note: after places the skin complaint following the letter for time

parts.note: a rash is an outbreak on the skin

explanation.surface: Clearing up a skin problem after a while.
explanation.definitionFit: In informal American use to trash something is to throw it away or destroy it, discarding it.

clue.text: Aussie's toilet with bad smell involved, additionally

indicators.note: involved means wrapped up within, so the smell sits inside the toilet word

parts.note: toot is Australian slang for a lavatory
BO is body odour

explanation.surface: An Australian lavatory with a nasty whiff thrown in as well.
explanation.walkthrough: The toilet word is Australian slang, which few solvers outside Australia will know; 'involved' signals the smell going inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means as well or besides, an idiom for in addition.

clue.text: Shooters around headland giving comfort

indicators.note: around here means turned round, so the word for shooters is read backwards

parts.note: guns are shooters, as in pistols or rifles
a ness is a promontory or headland, as in Loch Ness's neighbour Dungeness

explanation.surface: Riflemen gathered on a cape find it cosy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' looks like it means surrounding the headland, but here it signals turning the shooters word round.
explanation.definitionFit: Being snug means being warm and cosy, so the noun is a synonym for cosiness or ease.

clue.text: Groom's had some food following niceties at the start

indicators.note: following puts the food word after the initial letter
at the start means only the opening letter of the word is used

parts.note: eaten means having consumed some food

explanation.surface: A bridegroom has eaten after the opening pleasantries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groom' looks like the man at a wedding, but it is the verb meaning to tidy.
explanation.definitionFit: To groom is to make tidy or smart, the same as tidying up one's appearance.

clue.text: Write graffiti signature on government building

parts.note: to pen is to write
a tag is a graffiti artist's stylised signature

explanation.surface: Spray-painting a tag on a public building.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pentagon is the headquarters of the US Department of Defense in Virginia.

clue.text: Money abroad hidden by haggard relative

indicators.note: hidden by means held inside, so the money word sits within the haggard word

parts.note: gaunt means haggard or drawn
the rand is the currency of South Africa, a foreign money

explanation.surface: Cash overseas concealed by a worn-out family member.
explanation.definitionFit: A great-aunt, a parent's aunt, is a family member, so relative covers the term.

clue.text: I falsely report one of us

parts.note: to slander is to make false damaging statements about someone

explanation.surface: Someone admits to lying about a fellow member of the group.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's 'us' are the British, who live on islands, so any of them fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain is an island nation, so a British setter can describe any of its people as island-dwellers.

clue.text: His end to get excited?

indicators.note: excited letters are agitated, so the three words before are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: Asking whether a man's aim in life is just to have fun.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the anagram of HIS END TO, and a description of a pleasure-seeker's aim.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleasure-seeker lives for enjoyment, so their goal in life is thrills and excitement.

clue.text: New bags — they were originally made for consumers in Asia

definitions.text: they were originally made for consumers in Asia

parts.note: bags of something means lots, the same as oodles

explanation.surface: Fresh bags first manufactured for Asian shoppers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bags' looks like carrier bags, but it is the British informal word for plenty.
explanation.definitionFit: These pasta strands originated in China and East Asia, where they were first made as food.

clue.text: Composer taking transport back around Australia

indicators.note: around means the reversed word encloses the country
taking back means the transport word is read in reverse

parts.note: a tram is a form of public transport
Oz is the informal name for Australia

explanation.surface: A musician travels around Australia by tram.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses the transport word, giving MART, and 'around' puts that round the country's nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was an Austrian writer of classical music, a famous example of the category.

clue.text: Working around very small Greek character

indicators.note: around means the working word encloses the small word

parts.note: a machine that is on is working
micro means very small

explanation.surface: Busy with a tiny Greek person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'character' looks like a person, but it means a letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Omicron is the fifteenth letter of the Greek alphabet, the short O.

clue.text: Graduate, learner with decent headwear

parts.note: BA is a Bachelor of Arts, a graduate
L stands for learner, as on British learner-driver plates
moral means decent or upright

explanation.surface: A graduate and a learner driver wearing respectable hats.
explanation.walkthrough: A balmoral is a Scottish brimless bonnet, named after the royal castle in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: The balmoral is a flat Scottish cap, so it is a kind of hat.

clue.text: Showing signs of age, told story about introduction of nylon

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the story word goes round the opening letter

parts.note: to tell a story can mean to lie, as children say

indicators.note: the introduction of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: An old person spinning a tale about when nylon first arrived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'told story' looks like narration, but it means told a fib.
explanation.definitionFit: A face with wrinkles is described as lined, a common visible sign of getting older.

clue.text: Heavy diamonds collected by digger

indicators.note: collected by means taken inside, so the diamonds letter sits within the digger word

parts.note: a miner digs for coal or ore
D is the card-game abbreviation for diamonds

explanation.surface: A weighty load of diamonds gathered by a miner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavy' looks like an adjective, but it is the noun for a hired bodyguard.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy is informal for a muscular bodyguard or henchman, the same job as a minder.

clue.text: What can show how to get around mounting junk mail

indicators.note: mounting in a down clue means rising, so the word is read from bottom to top

parts.words: What can show how to get around
parts.note: maps are what can show you the way when travelling

explanation.surface: A tin can apparently showing how to get about, rising above unwanted post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What can' hints at the tinned meat of the same name, but the definition is 'junk mail'.
explanation.definitionFit: Unsolicited bulk email is called spam, after a Monty Python sketch about the tinned meat.

clue.text: Passage from some Mexican alehouse

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A route taken from a bar in Mexico.
explanation.definitionFit: A canal is an artificial waterway, a channel by which boats pass, so a passage.

clue.text: Digression put reader off

indicators.note: off means wrong or not right, so the letters of the two words before are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tangent that puts the reader off.
explanation.definitionFit: A departure from a topic is a move away from it, the same as wandering off the subject.

clue.text: Insult lawbreaker briefly with note to show intolerance

parts.note: to dis someone is slang for insulting them

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: a criminal breaks the law
te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: Insulting an offender with a written note to show prejudice.
explanation.definitionFit: To discriminate is to treat people unfairly because of prejudice, which is acting with bigotry.
